strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea of leveraging pretrained multi-view diffusion models both as a 2D→3D feature extractor and as a source of synthetic multi-view supervision, enabling training from single-view image collections without cameras, multi-view capture, or manual 3D annotations — a genuinely underexplored problem.

Demonstrates broad qualitative generalization across humans, dogs, and out-of-domain animal species (giraffe, rhino, horse, zebra) as well as non-human GSO objects, despite training on a single category/dataset, which is a compelling practical benefit.

The pipeline for turning predicted keypoints/edge graphs into an animatable rig (via MST extraction and Gaussian-based skinning) for 3D objects reconstructed from diffusion-generated views is a useful downstream application that showcases the alignment between predicted structure and the underlying 3D generative model's coordinate frame.

Ablations (diffusion features vs. ResNet features, number of virtual viewpoints) support the core claim that diffusion-derived multi-view features carry useful geometric priors beyond what a standard feature extractor obtains from the same generated images.
Clear presentation of the technical pipeline (feature aggregation, 3D unprojection, integral regression, multi-view reconstruction loss) with reasonably detailed equations.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is essentially limited to Human3.6M; despite substantial emphasis on animal/cross-species generalization (Stanford Dogs, AP-10K, GSO, DAVIS), no quantitative metrics (e.g., PCK, regression error against any pseudo/partial ground truth) are reported for these settings, so the strong generalization claims rest solely on qualitative figures.

On Human3.6M, the reported gains over the closest single-view baseline (Honari et al. [11], single-view) are modest and inconsistent across configurations (e.g., 130.58 vs 125.73 MPJPE with Linear regression for the 32-keypoint models is actually worse for some settings), weakening the claim of clearly outperforming prior single-view unsupervised methods.

The method still requires a fixed target camera-parameter set for the multi-view diffusion model to generate novel views; the paper does not clearly explain how these camera poses are chosen/fixed across training and whether this constitutes implicit camera information that is not truly 'camera-free,' which could be seen as tempering the 'no camera parameters' claim.

Computational cost is not quantified: iterative denoising to extract intermediate features plus generation of K views for both training and inference presumably incurs substantial runtime/memory overhead relative to feed-forward baselines, but no timing/throughput comparison is provided, limiting assessment of practicality.

Ablation study in the main text is narrow (only two axes: feature source and number of views), with more comprehensive ablations deferred to (unseen) supplementary material, making it hard to fully judge sensitivity to design choices such as timestep τ, grid resolution M, or number of keypoints N.

No failure-case analysis beyond a brief qualitative limitations paragraph; given the reliance on the diffusion model's generation quality, a more systematic study of failure modes (e.g., under strong articulation, occlusion, or unusual object shapes) would strengthen the paper's claims of robustness.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: code is promised but not yet released, and some architectural specifics (e.g., exact configuration of ϕ_kp, ϕ_vol, and the reconstruction network) are not fully detailed in the main paper.

strengths: The core idea of exploiting a pretrained multi-view diffusion model's implicit 3D geometric prior to supervise monocular 3D keypoint discovery, removing the need for calibrated multi-view capture, is a reasonable and potentially useful direction that extends prior 2D diffusion-feature keypoint work (StableKeypoints) and multi-view unprojection-based pose estimation to a monocular, annotation-free setting.

The overall pipeline (diffusion feature aggregation, 3D unprojection/volume construction, integral regression, edge-map-based reconstruction supervision) is clearly described and technically coherent, building sensibly on established components (Diffusion Hyperfeatures, learnable triangulation/volumetric aggregation, integral pose regression).

The paper demonstrates qualitative generalization across humans, dogs, and several unseen animal species/out-of-domain objects from a model trained on a single narrow domain (e.g., Human3.6M-trained model tested on GSO/DAVIS), and the extension to animatable rigging/skinning via MST and Gaussian skinning weights is a nice practical add-on.

Ablations on the use of diffusion features versus a ResNet baseline and on the number of generated views are informative and show the diffusion feature extractor is a meaningful component rather than an incidental choice.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is essentially limited to Human3.6M; all claims about generalization to animals (Stanford Dogs, AP-10K) and out-of-domain objects (GSO, DAVIS) are supported only qualitatively with no metrics (e.g., PCK, keypoint consistency, or any proxy ground truth), which is insufficient to substantiate the paper's central generalization claims given this is a major selling point of the work.

On Human3.6M, the method's improvement over the most comparable single-view baseline (Honari et al., single-view) is modest (e.g., P-MPJPE 85.3 vs 89.1), and the method trails substantially behind multi-view counterparts (e.g., Honari et al. 4-view: 63.0 P-MPJPE vs ours ~85), undercutting the 'competitive with multi-view' framing in the text; the comparison set also omits more recent/stronger unsupervised or weakly-supervised monocular baselines.

The 'unsupervised, no camera parameters' framing is somewhat overstated: the multi-view diffusion backbone (SV3D) is conditioned on and generates views for a fixed, known set of target camera poses, so the method does rely on known relative camera geometry for its generated supervision signal; this should be clarified rather than presented as fully camera-free.

The method's generalization performance is likely substantially inherited from SV3D's own pretrained generative prior (trained on large 3D/multi-view datasets) rather than solely from the proposed keypoint discovery scheme; there is no ablation disentangling how much of the cross-domain generalization is attributable to the backbone's prior versus the proposed aggregation/lifting method, making the contribution's novelty and robustness harder to assess.

No quantitative or efficiency analysis is given for the computational cost acknowledged in the limitations (multi-step denoising for feature extraction), despite this being flagged as a key limitation; a runtime/memory comparison against multi-view and feed-forward baselines would be needed to judge practicality.

The animatable object manipulation pipeline (Section 3.4/4.4) is presented only through qualitative figures with no quantitative or user-study evaluation of rig quality, deformation plausibility, or comparison to manual/automatic rigging baselines.

Minor robustness concerns are not analyzed: failure cases when the diffusion model generates geometrically inconsistent views (acknowledged as a limitation) are not quantified, and there is no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters such as number of keypoints N, voxel resolution M, or timestep τ beyond the single ablation on view count and feature choice.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: repurposing a pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D) both as a synthetic multi-view supervision source and as a 3D-aware feature extractor for unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery, removing the need for calibrated multi-view capture or manual 3D annotations.

The pipeline is conceptually clean: diffusion feature aggregation -> unprojection into a canonical 3D volume -> integral regression for keypoints -> multi-view reconstruction loss using diffusion-generated views as pseudo ground truth, with a learnable structural (edge) graph.

Strong demonstrated generalization: a model trained only on Human3.6M produces plausible keypoints on DAVIS (in-the-wild) and GSO (out-of-domain non-human objects); a model trained on Stanford Dogs generalizes to unseen breeds and to unseen species on AP-10K (giraffe, rhino, zebra, horse), which is compelling evidence that the diffusion-derived 3D priors transfer across categories.

Quantitative results on Human3.6M show the method outperforms prior single-view unsupervised baselines (KeypointNet, Honari et al. single-view) and is competitive with some 2-view multi-view baselines, despite using only a single image at both train and test time.

The ablations (diffusion features vs. ResNet features, number of generated views) are informative and support the core claim that diffusion features specifically (not just multi-view diffusion images) drive the accuracy gains.

An additional, useful downstream application (animatable 3D object generation via MST-based skeleton extraction and Gaussian-based skinning) showcases practical utility beyond pure keypoint accuracy and leverages the same diffusion-aligned representation without extra registration.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is narrow: only Human3.6M has numerical metrics (MPJPE/N-MPJPE/P-MPJPE); Stanford Dogs, AP-10K, DAVIS, and GSO results are qualitative only, so claims of accurate cross-category keypoint discovery are not rigorously substantiated (e.g., no PCK-style or keypoint-consistency metric for animals).

The "Ours*" result on a simplified 6-action subset is compared against Yang et al.*, but it is unclear the two subsets/protocols are truly equivalent, making this specific comparison potentially misleading if not carefully matched.

The method still trails the strongest multi-view unsupervised baseline (Honari et al., 4-view, 2-hid MLP: 73.8 MPJPE) by a large margin (Ours: ~119-121 MPJPE), so the framing as "competitive with multi-view baselines" is somewhat optimistic beyond the specific 2-view BKinD-3D comparison.

No runtime/computational cost analysis is reported despite the method requiring multiple denoising steps per inference (T up to 1000, evaluated to timestep 500) plus multi-view generation, which the paper itself flags as a limitation but does not quantify (e.g., inference latency vs. feed-forward baselines).

Dependence on external preprocessing (Grounded SAM for foreground masking) and on the fidelity of the pretrained SV3D-p model introduces failure modes (acknowledged only qualitatively in the Limitations section) that are not analyzed with concrete failure-case examples or error statistics.

The paper does not discuss how the fixed number of keypoints (N=18/32) is chosen per object category, nor whether/how discovered keypoints semantically align across very different categories (human vs. dog vs. giraffe), which is relevant given the cross-category generalization claims.

Limited comparison to very recent unsupervised 2D/3D keypoint discovery methods beyond the specific set cited (e.g., no comparison to more contemporary equivariance- or video-based unsupervised 3D approaches), and the related work on diffusion-based keypoint methods is restricted essentially to a single prior work (StableKeypoints), understating the breadth of the diffusion-feature literature for downstream comparison.

The reconstruction network architecture and further training details (e.g., network capacity, exact layer structure) are not fully specified in the main text, which could hamper reproducibility without the supplementary material.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: leveraging a pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D) both as a source of synthetic multi-view supervision and as a geometry-aware feature extractor for unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery, removing the need for calibrated multi-view capture or 3D annotations.

Technically sound pipeline: diffusion feature aggregation across layers, unprojection into a 3D volumetric representation, differentiable integral regression for keypoint localization, and a multi-view reconstruction loss with edge-map structural cues form a coherent, end-to-end differentiable system.

Strong empirical support: quantitative results on Human3.6M (competitive with/better than several multi-view and monocular baselines using only a single view), CUB-200-2011 2D projections, and qualitative results on Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, and AP-10K demonstrate good cross-category and out-of-domain generalization.

Extensive and informative ablations (Table 3 and supplementary Table 5) covering backbone choice, 3D lifting strategy, number of virtual viewpoints, keypoint count, diffusion timestep, data quantity, affine augmentation, view misalignment robustness, and aggregation strategy, which substantiate individual design choices.
Useful downstream application (animatable 3D object generation with skinning weights derived from predicted keypoints/edges) that showcases practical value beyond keypoint accuracy alone.

Reasonably transparent reporting of failure cases (left-right ambiguity, dependency on diffusion model quality) and honest discussion of reproducibility issues in baseline comparisons (CUB baseline reproduction appendix), which strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: Reliance on a single multi-view diffusion backbone (SV3D) raises questions about generality of the claims; the method's accuracy is explicitly coupled to the diffusion model's generation quality, as acknowledged in the failure case discussion, but no experiments with alternative multi-view diffusion backbones are shown in the main paper.

Quantitative comparison on CUB and Stanford Dogs is limited to projected 2D metrics rather than true 3D evaluation, since no 3D ground truth exists for these datasets; the paper explicitly states these 2D projections 'do not fully reflect the strengths of 3D predictions,' leaving the core 3D claims for non-human categories only qualitatively supported.

The number of keypoints (N=18) and their semantic identity are not consistently interpretable or validated against a canonical keypoint definition, and no quantitative keypoint correspondence/consistency metric (e.g., PCK across identity or cross-instance semantic consistency) is reported for animal categories.

Computational overhead is significant (diffusion generation and feature extraction), which is acknowledged (Table 6) but limits the immediate practicality of the method compared to lightweight baselines, and the trade-off is not deeply analyzed against accuracy gains.

Ablation and main experiments are conducted only on Human3.6M for quantitative studies; broader quantitative ablation on animal datasets is missing, so the generalization advantages claimed for CUB/Stanford Dogs rest mainly on qualitative figures.
The left-right ambiguity failure mode is a fairly fundamental limitation of the self-supervised formulation and is not addressed with any mitigation strategy, only reported as a known issue.

Some technical details (e.g., exact choice/justification of the aggregation weights, robustness of the Minimum Spanning Tree skeleton extraction for non-tree biological structures, sensitivity to keypoint count across categories) could be elaborated further for full reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: unsupervised 3D keypoint discovery from a single image without calibrated multi-view data, 3D annotations, or category-specific priors, by exploiting multi-view diffusion priors (SV3D) as a geometry-aware feature extractor and pseudo-supervision source.

The pipeline design (diffusion feature aggregation across layers, unprojection into an explicit 3D volumetric representation, integral regression for differentiable keypoint localization, Gaussian-line edge rendering for structural cues) is technically coherent and well-motivated.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation spanning humans (Human3.6M), birds (CUB-200-2011), dogs (Stanford Dogs), and several out-of-domain/in-the-wild test sets (DAVIS, GSO, AP-10K), demonstrating cross-category generalization not typically shown in prior unsupervised 3D keypoint work.

Thorough ablation studies (2D backbone choice, 3D lifting strategy, number of virtual viewpoints, number of keypoints, diffusion timestep, training data scale, affine augmentation necessity, robustness to view misalignment, view aggregation strategy), which substantiate several design choices.

Transparent reporting of reproducibility issues for CUB-align baselines (showing both original and re-trained numbers) and inclusion of explicit failure-case analysis (left-right ambiguity, dependency on diffusion-generated view quality), which strengthens scientific credibility.

The downstream animatable 3D object pipeline (skeleton extraction, skinning weights, articulation) is a useful demonstration that the discovered keypoints carry meaningful structural and connectivity information beyond raw localization accuracy.
Computational cost analysis (Table 6) is provided, giving a candid account of the overhead introduced by the diffusion-based pipeline relative to prior keypoint discovery methods.
weaknesses: Quantitative 3D evaluation is restricted to Human3.6M; for CUB and Stanford Dogs (and all out-of-domain sets) the paper offers only qualitative results or indirect 2D-projected keypoint comparisons, so the core claim of accurate 3D keypoint discovery for non-human/animal categories is not rigorously substantiated with numeric 3D metrics.

No quantitative measure of cross-instance semantic keypoint consistency (e.g., a PCK-style metric verifying that keypoint index n consistently corresponds to the same semantic part across different object instances/poses) is reported, which is a standard and important criterion for unsupervised keypoint discovery papers.

On Human3.6M, the method's single-view performance, while competitive with other unsupervised monocular methods, remains clearly worse than multi-view-supervised approaches (e.g., Honari et al. with more views/keypoints reaches much lower MPJPE), so the practical accuracy gain over the state of the art is limited to a narrow unsupervised-monocular niche.

The entire framework is bottlenecked by the quality and consistency of a single pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D); the paper's own failure-case analysis shows that inconsistent or degraded diffusion-generated views (e.g., view flipping, hallucinated occluded regions) directly corrupt keypoint predictions, and there is no mitigation strategy beyond noting the issue.

The pipeline is a complex, multi-stage system (foreground segmentation via Grounded-SAM, SV3D multi-view generation, diffusion feature extraction/aggregation, 3D volumetric lifting, Gaussian Frosting reconstruction, MST-based skeleton extraction, Gaussian skinning), which raises reproducibility concerns and makes it difficult to isolate the source of errors or to compare fairly with simpler baselines.

The unresolved left–right ambiguity is a fundamental limitation for any downstream application requiring consistent semantic lateralization (e.g., limb-specific manipulation), and the paper does not explore or discuss possible remedies (e.g., incorporating weak semantic priors).

Inference-time computational cost is substantially higher than prior keypoint discovery methods (Table 6), which may limit practical applicability, and the paper does not report training-time cost or wall-clock comparisons against baselines beyond the brief mention of 20k training steps.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: leveraging pretrained multi-view diffusion priors (SV3D) to supervise unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery, removing the need for calibrated multi-view data or 3D annotations.

Clean technical pipeline: diffusion feature aggregation across layers/views, unprojection into a 3D volumetric representation, and a self-supervised multi-view reconstruction loss with edge-map structural cues are all clearly described and reasonably justified.

Strong and broad empirical validation: quantitative results on Human3.6M (competitive with/superior to multi-view baselines despite using single-view input) and CUB-200-2011, plus qualitative generalization to Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, and AP-10K across a wide range of object categories including out-of-domain species.

Thorough ablations (backbone choice, 3D lifting strategy, number of virtual viewpoints, number of keypoints, diffusion timestep, training data size, affine augmentation, view misalignment robustness, view aggregation strategy) that support the design decisions and demonstrate robustness.

An interesting downstream application (animatable 3D object generation with skinning weights derived from predicted keypoints/edges) that showcases practical usefulness of the discovered keypoints beyond just accuracy metrics.

Reasonably honest reporting: includes a failure case analysis (left-right ambiguity, dependency on diffusion model quality) and discusses reproducibility issues in baseline comparisons on CUB, attempting fair re-evaluation with official code.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation for 3D accuracy is limited essentially to a single dataset (Human3.6M); other datasets (CUB, Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, AP-10K) are evaluated only qualitatively or via projected 2D proxies, so the core claim of accurate 3D keypoint discovery across diverse categories is not rigorously quantified beyond humans.

The method relies heavily on the quality of a specific pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D); the failure-case analysis itself shows that diffusion generation errors (e.g., inconsistent or flipped multi-view outputs, poor occluded-region synthesis) directly propagate into keypoint errors, and no other diffusion backbones are tested, raising a generalizability/robustness concern.

Computational cost at inference/training appears substantial (diffusion denoising, multi-view feature extraction) compared to lightweight prior unsupervised keypoint methods; while an ablation table addresses this, the practical overhead versus benefit trade-off could be discussed more explicitly in the main text.

The number of keypoints N is a fixed hyperparameter without a principled or learned criterion for correspondence to semantically meaningful parts across very different object categories (e.g., birds vs. dogs vs. humans use different N), and no analysis of cross-instance keypoint consistency/correspondence stability is given quantitatively.

The left-right ambiguity failure mode is inherent to self-supervised keypoint learning and not resolved, which could limit downstream usefulness (e.g., in animation or precise pose analysis) without additional disambiguation cues.

Some evaluation protocol choices (e.g., 3D annotation-free CUB/Stanford Dogs evaluated by projecting to 2D, and known difficulties reproducing prior 2D baselines) make some comparisons less than fully rigorous, though the authors do attempt to mitigate this via reproduction experiments in the appendix.
